![Design-step trajectories and final designs in the latent design space (PC1/PC2 of six design features), explored by each of the three agentic design systems. Each system covers a distinguishable region, with CRDAL converging toward the area of highest design capacity. Figure 8 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"}

In *Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design* [[1]](#ref-1), [Zeda Xu](https://www.linkedin.com/in/zedaxu/), [Nikolas Martelaro](https://nikmart.com/), and [Christopher McComb](https://cmccomb.com/) at Carnegie Mellon test whether adding a second LLM agent that watches the first agent's reasoning beats a self-monitoring single agent on a constrained engineering design task.

> The engineering design research community has studied agentic AI systems that use Large Language Model (LLM) agents to automate the engineering design process. However, these systems are prone to some of the same pathologies that plague humans. Just as human designers, LLM design agents can fixate on existing paradigms and fail to explore alternatives when solving design challenges, potentially leading to suboptimal solutions. In this work, we propose (1) a novel *Self-Regulation Loop (SRL)*, in which the Design Agent self-regulates and explicitly monitors its own metacognition, and (2) a novel *Co-Regulation Design Agentic Loop (CRDAL)*, in which a *Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agent assists the Design Agent in metacognition to mitigate design fixation*, thereby improving system performance for engineering design tasks. In the battery pack design problem examined here, we found that *the novel CRDAL system generates designs with better performance, without significantly increasing the computational cost*, compared to a plain Ralph Wiggum Loop (RWL) and the metacognitively self-assessing Self-Regulation Loop (SRL). Also, we found that the CRDAL system navigated through the latent design space more effectively than both SRL and RWL. However, *the SRL did not generate designs with significantly better performance than RWL*, even though it explored a different region of the design space. The proposed system architectures and findings of this work provide practical implications for future development of agentic AI systems for engineering design.

## Method

![System flowchart of the Co-Regulation Design Agentic Loop (CRDAL): a Design Agent runs the iterative design loop while a separate Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agent inspects each step's progress trace and feeds back strategic suggestions. Figure 5 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure5.png){fig-align="center"}

How the three loops differ:

- **RWL.** Design Agent generates a candidate design, a numerical evaluator/validator scores it, raw feedback ("failed thermal constraint, current capacity is X") goes back to the Design Agent, which reflects implicitly and tries again.
- **SRL.** RWL plus two additions: a non-LLM Progress Analyzer summarizes the design history (capacity trend, which past attempts were valid), and the Design Agent is explicitly prompted to set goals, identify the bottleneck constraint, and plan strategy. Still one agent doing both designing and metacognizing.
- **CRDAL.** SRL but the metacognition is moved to a separate LLM agent. The same Progress Analyzer summary now feeds a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agent, which writes strategic notes about the Design Agent's progress (assessment of "improving / stalling / regressing", bottleneck identification, suggestion for the next iteration) and passes them to the Design Agent alongside the raw numerical feedback. Same kind of metacognitive content as SRL's self-prompts; the difference is that another agent produces it.

## Results

The design task is to lay out 18650 lithium-ion cells (the cylindrical batteries inside laptops, vapes, and Tesla packs, at 3.7 V and 2.5 Ah each) into a 400 V pack of at least 25 Ah, while keeping the pack under 60 °C and able to deliver 48 A continuously. Higher Ah means longer runtime at a given current. Across 30 runs per system on this task using Gemini 3.1 Pro, the CRDAL design agent reached a mean capacity of 70.92 Ah, versus 54.14 Ah for the self-monitoring SRL and 49.31 Ah for the plain Ralph Wiggum Loop (RWL). All three were well above the 25 Ah floor in every case. The gap between SRL and RWL was not statistically significant. CRDAL did not use more design steps than the other two systems.

![Battery pack capacity by agentic design system, $n=30$ runs each. CRDAL beats both RWL ($p < 0.001$, Cohen's $d = 1.375$) and SRL ($p = 0.001$, $d = 0.955$); SRL is statistically indistinguishable from RWL. Figure 6 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure6.png){fig-align="center"}

A note on the name: Ralph Wiggum is a recurring child character in *The Simpsons*, known for being cheerfully oblivious and confidently wrong without self-correcting. The "Ralph Wiggum Loop" is a software-engineering term of art for an agent that retries until external validation passes, with no self-assessment of its own attempts.

## My Notes

- **The SRL ≈ RWL result is the headline finding.** A growing body of work argues that LLMs cannot reliably correct their own reasoning without an external signal. Huang et al. find self-correction either flat or actively harmful on reasoning benchmarks once the answer-verification crutch is removed [[2]](#ref-2). Apple's [SelfReflect](/posts/20260430-selfreflect-internal-distribution/) [[5]](#ref-5) extends the pattern to uncertainty self-reports: 20 modern LLMs cannot faithfully summarize their own internal answer distributions without sample-augmented context. This paper supplies a clean engineering-design data point in the same direction: telling an agent to "monitor your metacognition" gave it a different exploration trajectory but no better outcomes than just retrying. The reflective loop has to be closed by something the agent isn't.

- **The SRL-vs-CRDAL comparison narrows what matters.** SRL already gives the Design Agent explicit metacognitive prompts (assess progress, identify the bottleneck, plan strategy) plus a history summary. CRDAL keeps that same metacognitive content but moves it to a different LLM agent that writes the strategic notes about the Design Agent's progress instead of asking the Design Agent to write them about itself. The CRDAL ≫ SRL gap (Cohen's d = 0.955) therefore isolates the agent split as what mattered, not the explicitness of the metacognitive prompts, which SRL already had. This converges with Wan et al.'s [ReMA](/posts/20260430-rema-meta-think/), which decouples reasoning into a meta-thinker and an executor and trains them jointly with multi-agent RL, beating single-agent reasoning baselines on math [[3]](#ref-3). The same direction of result holds in competitive math and in engineering design, which makes the underlying claim harder to dismiss as task-specific: metacognition needs to come from a different head than the one doing the work.

- **One task, one model, n=30. Generalization is the open question.** The authors own this in §4.3: a single battery-pack optimization with one frontier model is a thin base for a system-architecture claim. Adding a Co-Regulation Agent introduces a new agent-to-agent communication channel that this benchmark, by design, does not stress, and that channel is exactly where multi-agent systems tend to break in their own characteristic ways, as the [MAST taxonomy](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/) catalogs across 200+ failure traces. The interesting follow-up is not "does CRDAL beat RWL on more tasks" but "where does CRDAL break in ways that RWL doesn't."

- **From the intrinsic-metacognitive-learning side, CRDAL is a ceiling.** [Liu and van der Schaar argue in their position paper](/posts/20260430-intrinsic-metacognitive-learning/) that today's "self-improving" agents almost all rely on extrinsic metacognition: fixed, human-designed loops where the metacognitive structure is wired in by the system designer rather than learned by the agent [[4]](#ref-4). They contend genuinely scalable self-improvement needs intrinsic metacognitive learning: the agent itself deciding what to evaluate, what to reflect on, what to learn next. CRDAL is a clean example of the extrinsic kind: a hand-designed second agent in a hand-designed role, with the loop topology fixed by the authors. The Ralph Wiggum result is real, but read alongside the position paper it is evidence that extrinsic scaffolding helps right now, not that this is the architecture self-improving agents will eventually settle on.
